problem:
Harbour Energy sends its monthly direct debit collections on the 25th of each month, and the billing team has always assumed that generating the collection file is the same as notifying the customer. In March, a billing change moved 8,000 customers to a new tariff, changing their collection amounts, but the pre-notification emails for the new amounts were never sent because the notification job failed silently. The collections were submitted on time and debited on the due date, and hundreds of customers complained that money had been taken without warning at an amount they did not expect. Several demanded refunds, and the customer service team had no evidence that any notice had been sent.

Pre-notification and collection submission are two different obligations on two different timelines. Pre-notification is the creditor telling the debtor, at the latest 14 calendar days before the due date, what will be collected and when, or a different period where the mandate or agreement validly provides for one. Collection submission is the creditor PSP sending the collection into the interbank chain, and for SDD Core the submission deadline is D-1, one Inter-PSP Business Day before the due date. A file can be submitted perfectly on D-1 and still be wrong, because the debtor was never told.

Harbour Energy needs to separate the two timelines in its systems and its controls: a notification step with its own content, date and delivery evidence, and a submission step with its own deadline, each checked independently before the collection proceeds. A change to the amount or the date restarts the notification question, and a missing notice must delay the collection rather than be discovered after the debit.
solution:
Separate the two timelines in the design, in the data and in the controls. The pre-notification step records the content, the amount, the due date, the channel, the date sent and the delivery evidence for each debtor, and it is checked against the rule that notice must be given at the latest 14 calendar days before the due date, or within any different period validly agreed in the mandate. The submission step records the file generation date, the validation result and the submission to the creditor PSP against the D-1 deadline, one Inter-PSP Business Day before the due date. Neither step may be treated as proof of the other.

Build a gate between them. A collection becomes eligible for submission only when both conditions are true: the notice for that exact amount and due date has been sent and evidenced, and the submission deadline can still be met. If the amount or the due date changes after the notice was sent, the notice is no longer valid for the changed collection and a new notice is required, unless a validly agreed arrangement covers the change. If the notification job fails, the collections it covered are held automatically, and the failure alerts Operations instead of failing silently.

Finally, keep the evidence where a dispute can find it. Store the notice content, date and delivery evidence alongside the mandate and the collection, so a customer who disputes a debit can be shown exactly what they were told and when. Report monthly on notice failures, late notices and collections delayed for notice reasons, and treat a silent notification failure as an incident, with a fix and a control that proves the job ran and delivered.

decision.question: You are the business analyst for Harbour Energy. A tariff change alters collection amounts for 8,000 customers, but the pre-notification emails for the new amounts were never sent because the notification job failed silently. The collection file is ready for submission on D-1. The billing manager wants to submit it on time and send the notices afterwards. What do you recommend?

options.label: A
options.detail: Submit the file on D-1 as planned and send the notices after the debit, since the submission deadline is the one that matters.

options.label: B
options.detail: Hold the affected collections, send the pre-notifications with the correct amounts, and reschedule the collections to a due date that respects the notice period.

options.label: C
options.detail: Submit the file without any notice and offer refunds to anyone who complains.

options.label: D
options.detail: Submit the file and reduce the amounts back to the old tariff so the old notice still applies.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because pre-notification is a separate obligation from submission: the debtor must be told at the latest 14 calendar days before the due date, and a changed amount needs a new notice. Submitting on D-1 does not cure a missing notice. Option A debits customers without warning. Option D changes the billing to fit a failed process. Option C collects without authority and creates refund volumes.

happy: Billing calculates the amount, the pre-notification is sent at the latest 14 calendar days before the due date with the correct amount and date, and delivery evidence is recorded. The collection passes the notice and mandate checks, is submitted by D-1, and is debited on the due date. The customer recognises the amount, and the collection reconciles cleanly.

negative.title: Notification delivery failure
negative.detail: The notification job fails silently and notices are never sent. Hold the affected collections automatically, alert Operations, fix the job, send the notices, and reschedule the collections to a due date that respects the notice period.

negative.title: Changed amount or date after notice
negative.detail: A tariff change alters the amount after the notice was sent. Treat the old notice as invalid for the changed collection, send a new notice with the new amount, and reschedule the collection if the notice period cannot be met.

negative.title: Customer disputes the notice
negative.detail: A debtor says they were not notified or were told a different amount. Produce the stored notice content, date and delivery evidence. If the evidence is missing or wrong, handle the collection under the applicable refund or return process and fix the evidence gap.

negative.title: Submission deadline missed while waiting for notice
negative.detail: The notice period pushes the due date later than planned. Move the due date rather than submitting late or skipping the notice. Tell the customer the revised due date in the notice itself.

technical: Model pre-notification as its own entity linked to the mandate and the collection, with fields for content, amount, due date, channel, sent timestamp and delivery evidence. Model submission as a separate event with its own timestamp and D-1 deadline check, computed against the Inter-PSP Business Day calendar. Gate collection generation on both conditions, and never let a submission event imply a notice event. If the amount or due date changes, version the notice and require a new one for the changed collection. Monitor the notification job with a success and delivery confirmation, not just a run log, so a silent failure is detected the same day. Keep the notice, the mandate version and the collection linked by correlation IDs.

accounting: A collection held for a missing notice never posts, so it appears in the held-items worklist rather than in the ledger, and the billing forecast must show the delayed cash separately from the collected cash. A collection debited without a valid notice may be refunded, and the refund is posted as a separate linked event with the reason recorded. Operations works from a notice-exception worklist with SLA targets for re-issue and rescheduling, and Finance tracks the value and volume of collections delayed for notice reasons each month. Customer service uses the stored notice evidence to answer disputes, and a dispute that cannot be evidenced is escalated to the mandate owner.
